title: How each pauri sums up
hook: each pauri gathers the saloks before it into a stanza of its own

segments.voice: Yesterday, gaarab, and your line: serve without argument. Did you leave out the sigh? It's a week's end: the thread of compassion, compassion, sootak, laaitbaaree, sweet speech, gaarab. Today, how the var holds all of them together. Day five hundred sixty.
screen: `SERVE WITHOUT ARGUMENT.` · `A WEEK: THREADS, PURITY, SPEECH, SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Climb a staircase in an old Punjabi house, or the steps down to the water at a gurdwara sarovar, and every step has a name: pauri. The same word is used for a ladder rung. And it's also the name for the stanzas you've been hearing for weeks without quite noticing them. Japji is built of pauris. So is every var in the Guru Granth Sahib. For three weeks we've mostly been listening to saloks, the short verses that tell of trees and threads and scales. Today we look at the steps they're sitting on.
screen: `A STEP DOWN TO THE WATER.` → `PAURI: A STEP, A RUNG.` → `THE STEPS UNDER THE SALOKS.`

segments.voice: A var, as we heard on day five hundred thirty-six, is an old Punjabi ballad form, sung about heroes and battles. Its stanzas are pauris, and in a var they march: each one a step forward in the story. The Guru Granth Sahib has twenty-two vars. In the Asa di Var, the pauris are Guru Nanak's, twenty-four of them, and they carry the main line of the poem: who the One is, how creation stands, what a true servant is like, what the Guru does. Then, in front of each pauri, sit two or more saloks. Some are Guru Nanak's, some Guru Angad's. Many scholars hold that the saloks were set beside the pauris when Guru Arjan compiled the Granth, gathered by theme so they'd open up the step that follows. So the shape works like this. The saloks wander. They look at a silk-cotton tree, a cartload of books, a thread, a kitchen. They make you see something. And then the pauri arrives, and gathers what you've just seen into one step forward. You've felt this already. Remember the pauri where Guru Nanak says he's a sacrifice to the True Guru, who put wisdom on his eyes. It came after saloks about show without substance. The saloks showed the problem, and the pauri named the turning. Here's why it matters for listening. When you hear the Asa di Var sung, you can feel the rhythm: wander, gather; wander, gather. Many small pictures, then one step up. It's a way of learning that doesn't rush. You don't climb the whole staircase at once. You take the next pauri.
screen: `A VAR: A BALLAD OF HEROES.` · `24 PAURIS, GURU NANAK'S.` · `SALOKS WANDER, THE PAURI GATHERS.` · `WANDER, GATHER; ONE STEP UP.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one pauri whole. If you have a gutka or an app with the Asa di Var, find any pauri and read it slowly, all the way through, in Gurmukhi or in translation. If you don't, hold in your mind the pauri from this week: the contented ones served, did good, ate little, broke the world's chains, and the One kept giving more. Let it sit as one step, complete. Breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end. The bell holds the time.
Pauri. A step, a ladder rung, and a stanza. In the Asa di Var, each of Guru Nanak's twenty-four pauris gathers the saloks before it into one step forward.
Your line: step by step. Today, when a big task feels like a whole staircase, name only the next step, and take it. Day five hundred sixty.

howItsDone: When Asa di Var is sung at dawn, ragis sing the saloks and then each pauri, and many Sikhs read the var from a gutka, pauri by pauri.

notes: Counts: 24 pauris in Asa di Var (all M1) and 22 vars in the Guru Granth Sahib; confirm.
'In front of each pauri sit two or more saloks': confirm for every pauri of Asa di Var.
The view that Guru Arjan placed the saloks with the pauris during compilation (1604) is attributed to 'many scholars'; confirm framing.
Pauri 13 example: the saloks before it are described as 'about show without substance' (simmal tree, empty bowing, and the salok on reading and ritual); confirm.
